<div class="pq" data-key="0">
<p class="pq-stem"><strong>1.</strong> Each quarter, mystery shoppers visit 40 of a wireless carrier&#x27;s 600 stores, drawn at random. Service across the stores has not changed in two years, yet the quarterly average score has ranged from 7.6 to 8.2 out of 10. What explains the movement?</p>
<div class="pq-opts">
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="0"><span class="pq-l">a.</span> Each quarter&#x27;s average comes from a different sample of stores</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="1"><span class="pq-l">b.</span> Bias in the sample mean makes the average drift around the true score</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="2"><span class="pq-l">c.</span> The true average score shifts a little from quarter to quarter</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="3"><span class="pq-l">d.</span> Skewed scores keep the average from settling on a single value</button>
</div>
<p class="pq-fb" aria-live="polite"></p>

<p class="pq-stem"><strong>2.</strong> A market research firm has two unbiased estimators of average weekly streaming hours per household. With 100 households, the diary-only estimator has a standard error of 0.6 hours, and the one that adds set-top box data has 0.3. Both standard errors fall with the square root of n. How many households would the diary-only estimator need to reach 0.3?</p>
<div class="pq-opts">
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="0"><span class="pq-l">a.</span> 200 households</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="1"><span class="pq-l">b.</span> 1,600 households</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="2"><span class="pq-l">c.</span> 50 households</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="3"><span class="pq-l">d.</span> 400 households</button>
</div>
<p class="pq-fb" aria-live="polite"></p>
<template class="pq-src">Slide: <a href="06-models-uncertainty-slides.html#/estimator-3-is-more-efficient-than-estimator-2">Estimator 3 is more efficient than estimator 2</a>.</template>

<div class="pq" data-key="1">
<p class="pq-stem"><strong>3.</strong> A bank estimates each branch&#x27;s default rate as a weighted average of the branch&#x27;s observed default rate and the national rate. The weight on the national rate is 20/(n + 20), where n is the branch&#x27;s number of loans. What happens to this estimator as n grows very large?</p>
<div class="pq-opts">
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="0"><span class="pq-l">a.</span> It converges to the national rate, so it is inconsistent</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="1"><span class="pq-l">b.</span> It converges to the branch&#x27;s true rate, so it is consistent</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="2"><span class="pq-l">c.</span> Its variance falls but its bias stays, so it is inconsistent</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="3"><span class="pq-l">d.</span> It cannot converge to the branch&#x27;s rate, since it is biased</button>
</div>
<p class="pq-fb" aria-live="polite"></p>
<template class="pq-src">Slide: <a href="06-models-uncertainty-slides.html#/all-three-estimators-are-consistent">All three estimators are consistent</a>.</template>
</div>
<div class="pq" data-key="3">
<p class="pq-stem"><strong>4.</strong> A consulting firm surveys its staff about padding billable hours. Each person privately flips a coin: heads, answer yes; tails, answer truthfully. The firm doubles the share answering yes and subtracts 100%. Across many surveys this estimator averages the true share. This year 48% said yes, giving an estimate of −4%. What should the firm conclude?</p>
<div class="pq-opts">
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="0"><span class="pq-l">a.</span> The estimator is biased this year, since a share cannot be negative</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="1"><span class="pq-l">b.</span> The estimator is inconsistent, since a consistent one stays within 0 to 100%</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="2"><span class="pq-l">c.</span> The coin flips were unfair, since fair flips cannot give a negative share</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="3"><span class="pq-l">d.</span> The method is sound, since chance alone can push the estimate below zero</button>
</div>
<p class="pq-fb" aria-live="polite"></p>
<template class="pq-src">Slide: <a href="06-models-uncertainty-slides.html#/estimator-3-is-more-efficient-than-estimator-2">Estimator 3 is more efficient than estimator 2</a>.</template>
</div>
<div class="pq" data-key="1">
<p class="pq-stem"><strong>5.</strong> A hotel chain forecasts nightly room demand from 60 predictors and two years of daily data. An analyst prefers least squares to ridge regression, which shrinks coefficients toward zero, because least squares is unbiased. What is wrong with the argument?</p>
<div class="pq-opts">
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="0"><span class="pq-l">a.</span> Bias affects the coefficient estimates but not the forecasts</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="1"><span class="pq-l">b.</span> Forecast error also includes variance, which ridge reduces</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="2"><span class="pq-l">c.</span> Least squares is biased, since 60 predictors overfit the data</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="3"><span class="pq-l">d.</span> Ridge is also unbiased once its penalty is chosen well</button>
</div>
<p class="pq-fb" aria-live="polite"></p>
<template class="pq-src">Slide: <a href="06-models-uncertainty-slides.html#/the-biasvariance-trade-off">The bias–variance trade-off</a>.</template>
</div>
<div class="pq" data-key="2">
<p class="pq-stem"><strong>6.</strong> A hospital system budgets next year&#x27;s total cost of care for about 8,000 uninsured patients. Cost per patient is right-skewed: most costs are small and a few are very large. Which statistic of cost per patient should the budget build on?</p>
<div class="pq-opts">
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="0"><span class="pq-l">a.</span> Either one, since both estimate the center of the costs</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="1"><span class="pq-l">b.</span> The median, since it is more efficient for skewed costs</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="2"><span class="pq-l">c.</span> The mean, since the total is patients times the mean cost</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="3"><span class="pq-l">d.</span> The median, since a few large costs bias the sample mean</button>
</div>
<p class="pq-fb" aria-live="polite"></p>
<template class="pq-src">Slide: <a href="06-models-uncertainty-slides.html#/the-median-can-be-more-efficient-than-the-mean">The median can be more efficient than the mean</a>.</template>
</div>

<p class="pq-stem"><strong>7.</strong> A manufacturer ranks its plants each year by mean workers&#x27; compensation cost per injury. <div class="pq-opts">
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="0"><span class="pq-l">a.</span> Rank plants by median cost per injury that year</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="1"><span class="pq-l">b.</span> Rank plants by mean cost per injury over two years</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="2"><span class="pq-l">c.</span> Rank only plants with at least 30 injuries that year</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="3"><span class="pq-l">d.</span> Rank plants by mean cost, shown with its standard error</button>
</div>

<p class="pq-stem"><strong>8.</strong> A fitness-studio franchisor wants to tell prospective owners the profit a new studio can expect in its first year. It has opened 900 studios, and 600 are still open. Studios that lose money usually close within two years. Which figure should it report?</p>
<div class="pq-opts">
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="0"><span class="pq-l">a.</span> Mean first-year profit of the 600 open studios, a full census of the network</button>

<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="2"><span class="pq-l">c.</span> Mean first-year profit of all 900 studios, including the 300 that closed</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="3"><span class="pq-l">d.</span> Mean first-year profit of 1,800 open studios in its brand and two sister brands</button>
</div>
<p class="pq-fb" aria-live="polite"></p>

<p class="pq-stem"><strong>9.</strong> A beverage distributor regresses log(cases ordered + 1) for each bar account and week on a promotion indicator by OLS. Many accounts order nothing in a given week. An analyst reruns it counting bottles instead of cases, at 24 bottles per case. What happens to the promotion coefficient?</p>
<div class="pq-opts">
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="0"><span class="pq-l">a.</span> It becomes undefined, since weeks with no orders have no logarithm</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="1"><span class="pq-l">b.</span> It stays the same, since a change of units shifts only the intercept</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="2"><span class="pq-l">c.</span> It is multiplied by 24, since each case becomes 24 bottles</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="3"><span class="pq-l">d.</span> It changes, since adding 1 means a different quantity in each unit</button>
</div>
<p class="pq-fb" aria-live="polite"></p>
<template class="pq-src">Slide: <a href="06-models-uncertainty-slides.html#/the-type-of-outcome-determines-the-model">The type of outcome determines the model</a>.</template>

<p class="pq-stem"><strong>10.</strong> A utility mails home energy reports to 400 of 800 households chosen at random and compares their electricity use the next month with the other 400. <div class="pq-opts">

<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="2"><span class="pq-l">c.</span> Shuffle usage within the report group, keeping the 400 labels fixed</button>
<button type="button" class="pq-opt" data-i="3"><span class="pq-l">d.</span> Repeat the mailing to a new random 400 homes, recording usage each time</button>
</div>

<script>
(function () {
  var qs = document.querySelectorAll('.pq'), first = 0, done = 0;
  var score = document.querySelector('.pq-score');
  function tally() { if (score) score.textContent = done ? ('Right on the first try: ' + first + ' of ' + done + ' answered (' + qs.length + ' questions).') : ''; }
  qs.forEach(function (q) {
    var keys = q.dataset.key.split(',');
    var fb = q.querySelector('.pq-fb'), src = q.querySelector('.pq-src');
    var tries = 0;
    q.querySelectorAll('.pq-opt').forEach(function (b) {
      b.addEventListener('click', function () {
        tries += 1;
        if (keys.indexOf(b.dataset.i) >= 0) {
          b.classList.add('pq-right');
          q.querySelectorAll('.pq-opt').forEach(function (x) { x.disabled = true; });
          fb.className = 'pq-fb pq-ok';
          fb.innerHTML = 'Correct. ' + (src ? src.innerHTML : '');
          done += 1; if (tries === 1) first += 1; tally();
        } else {
          b.classList.add('pq-wrong'); b.disabled = true;
          fb.className = 'pq-fb pq-no';
          fb.textContent = 'Not this one. Try again.';
        }
      });
    });
  });
})();
</script>
